q: Who led the English army in the Battle of Buxar?
solution:
The correct answer is Hector Munro. Key PointsBattle of Buxar:

• The Battle of Buxar occurred on 22nd October, 1764 on the banks of the Ganges River near Buxar, a city in the state of Bihar in India.

• The forces of three regional powers — Mir Qasim, the dethroned Nawab of Bengal; Shuja-ud-Daula, the Nawab of Awadh; and Shah Alam II, the Mughal emperor — formed an alliance against the British East India Company.

• Major Hector Munro led the Company's forces.

• Despite having larger forces, the Indian allies were defeated.

• Major reasons for their defeat, included discord between leaders, lack of strong centralized control, and the superior military strategy of the British forces.

• The battle marked a significant turning point in the history of India, as it affirmed the military supremacy of the East India Company over the Indian powers and set the background for their political power over the region.

• After the battle, the Treaty of Allahabad was signed in 1765.

• As per the treaty's terms, the East India Company acquired the rights for revenue collection (Diwani rights) in the provinces of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.

• These rights marked the beginning of the Company's formal rule in India.

• The treaty also stipulated the stationing of Company troops in Awadh to lend military assistance to the Nawab if required, which weakened the sovereignty of the region.

• The 1765 Treaty of Allahabad also required Nawab Shuja-ud-Daulah to pay Rs. 50 lakh as war indemnity which significantly weakened Awadh financially.

• The victory at Buxar gave the East India Company an immense boost in confidence and marked the beginning of British imperialism in India.

• Finally, the Battle of Buxar was significant because it was the first time the British fought in India for territorial gains and political power, as opposed to previous battles which were primarily fought over trade disputes.

q: Who sent the Greek ambassador Megasthenes to the court of Chandragupta Maurya?
solution:
The correct answer is Seleucus. Key Points

• Megasthenes was sent to the court of Chandragupta Maurya by Seleucus I Nicator.

• Seleucus I Nicator was one of the generals of Alexander the Great who, after Alexander's death, took control of the eastern part of his empire, which included territories in Asia Minor, Persia, and parts of India.

• Seleucus I Nicator and Chandragupta Maurya signed a treaty, following which Megasthenes was sent as an ambassador from the Seleucid Dynasty to the Mauryan Empire.

• Megasthenes is known for his important work "Indica," a record of his observations about India's geography, culture, and society.

Additional InformationMegasthenes wrote an account of his observations about India in his book named "Indica"..

• Geographical Details: Megasthenes provided an account of India's geography, including its mountains, rivers, flora and fauna, and climatic conditions.

• Description of Society: "Indica" included distinct details about social divisions, including the caste system and occupations of various groups.

• Urban Centers: Megasthenes described the city of Pataliputra (modern Patna), capital of the Maurya empire, in detail. This gave us information about city life, architecture, and administration.

• Administration and Military: The book portrayed the organized administrative structures and gave an account of the Mauryan army, with descriptions of elephants in warfare.

• Customs and Practices: "Indica" included information about contemporary customs, diets, festivals, and religious practices, and reported that India had no slavery.

• Megasthenes also provided an account of Chandragupta Maurya’s reign and wrote about the prosperity and peace within the empire.

• It is important to note that "Indica" had some inaccuracies or exaggerations possibly due to misunderstandings or cultural differences. For example, Megasthenes reported on creatures such as giant ants that dug up gold dust and humans with no mouths, which are widely considered to be based on misunderstandings or myths.

Chandragupta Maurya (ruled c. 321–c. 297 BCE) was the founder of the Maurya Empire in India. His reign was noted for its significant expansion, political unity, administration and development of infrastructure.

• Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the Nanda Dynasty in Magadh with the help of his advisor, Chanakya (Kautilya), and began his rule.

• He had a vast empire that included large parts of India, extending to Persia and parts of Afghanistan in the west.

• Chandragupta's administration was centralized. The Mauryan administration, as described in Kautilya's Arthashastra, had a highly organized bureaucratic structure with a council of ministers.

• He had a standing army and implemented an efficient revenue collection system.

• Chandragupta is said to have embraced Jainism towards the end of his life and undertook a fasting ritual until death, as per Jain tradition, at a place called Shravanabelagola in present-day Karnataka, India.

• Chandragupta's rule was succeeded by his son Bindusara, and then by his famous grandson, Ashoka.

q: In which year was the Vernacular Press Act enacted in British India?
solution:
The correct answer is 1878.

Key Points

• The Vernacular Press Act was enacted in British India in the year 1878.

• This law was enforced by the British to curtail the freedom of the Indian-language press.

• The Act was used to prevent the expression of criticism toward British policies, notably, the opposition that had grown with the outset of the Second Anglo-Afghan War (1878-80)

• It was enacted when Lord Lytton was Viceroy of India; he was known for his controversial and suppressive policies during his tenure.

• The act stated that any press printing in Vernacular language had to declare all its printing machinery and submit all material for scrutiny before publication. If the content was inflammable or criticised British authorities, it would result in the confiscation of the press.

• It was the first legislation to curtail press freedom in India, and the press became a medium of both control and revolt during British rule.

• The act provoked widespread criticism and protest by Indians. It eventually became one of the contributing factors to the nationalistic movements that emerged at the end of the 19th century.

• The Act was, however, repealed in 1882 by Lytton's successor, Lord Ripon, in a move to foster press freedom in India.

• The rule of the English East India Company ended in British India under the Government of India Act of 1858. Under this Act, the governance of India was transferred from the company to the British Crown, marking the start of the period of direct rule, also known as the British Raj.

key features of the Government of India Act of 1858:

• End of East India Company Rule: The Act, coming into force on 2 August 1858, ended the rule of the East India Company after nearly 250 years of control over Indian territories.

• Secretary of State for India: The Act introduced a new official post, the Secretary of State for India, who was a member of the British cabinet. He was given complete control over Indian administration and was aided by a 15-member Council of India.

• Change in Governance Structure: The Governor-General of India, who was now also identified as the Viceroy of India, was the representative of the Crown in India and was responsible for the executive administration of the Indian provinces. This change ended the old "double government" system where the Board of Control and the Court of Directors administrating different roles.

• Retention of Company Troops: Approximately 260,000 soldiers of the existing East India Company became soldiers of the Crown.

• End of Doctrine of Lapse: The 1858 Act ended the much-disputed Doctrine of Lapse, introduced by Lord Dalhousie in 1848, under which the British annexed any princely state whose ruler was either "manifestly incompetent" or died without a male heir.

• Legal Reform: With this transition, a comprehensive legal system was enforced, including the introduction of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) in 1860.

• Civil Services: The Act opened doors to the institutionalization of the Indian Civil Services. Although Indians could sit for the civil services examinations after this Act, until 1922. Indians could appear in the Indian Civil Service Examinations which were held in England.

Additional InformationWars:

• Anglo-Afghan Wars: These wars were fought between British India and Afghanistan. By 1858, the first of these wars (1839-1842) had already concluded with a humiliating retreat for the British. Two more Anglo-Afghan Wars would follow in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

• Anglo-Sikh Wars: There were two Anglo-Sikh Wars. The First Anglo-Sikh War (1845-46) and the Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848-49). As a result of these wars, the Sikh Empire was annexed by the British East India Company.

• Burma Wars: The Second Anglo-Burmese War (1852) led to the British East India Company's annexation of the lower Burma. The third war (1885) would result in the total annexation of Burma by the British.

Social Changes:

• Education Policies: The British tried to reform the education system, grounding it in Western philosophy and ideals. The University of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras were established in 1857.

• Social Reforms: Under the British rule, several old Indian social practices were challenged. For instance, the practice of Sati (the self-immolation of a widow on her husband's funeral pyre) was outlawed by Governor-General William Bentinck in 1829.

• Religious Changes: Christian missionaries were more freely allowed to propagate Christianity, leading to a growth of this minority religion in different parts of India.

• Infrastructure: Infrastructure, including roads and railways, telegraph and postal services were expanded, largely aimed at securing and supporting British military and administrative control.

• Introduction of the Railways: The first passenger railway in India was opened in 1853, prior to the Government of India Act, between Bombay and Thane.

q: Who among the following was the author of ‘Indica’, an account of India under the reign of the Maurya dynasty?
solution:
The correct answer is Megasthenes. Key Points

• The author of 'Indica' was Megasthenes.

• Seleucus I Nicator was one of the generals of Alexander the Great who, after Alexander's death, took control of the eastern part of his empire, which included territories in Asia Minor, Persia, and parts of India.

• His work 'Indica' is a significant source of information about India, providing valuable details about its geography, society, and culture during the Mauryan period.

Additional InformationMegasthenes wrote an account of his observations about India in his book named "Indica"..

• Geographical Details: Megasthenes provided an account of India's geography, including its mountains, rivers, flora and fauna, and climatic conditions.

• Description of Society: "Indica" included distinct details about social divisions, including the caste system and occupations of various groups.

• Urban Centers: Megasthenes described the city of Pataliputra (modern Patna), capital of the Maurya empire, in detail. This gave us information about city life, architecture, and administration.

• Administration and Military: The book portrayed the organized administrative structures and gave an account of the Mauryan army, with descriptions of elephants in warfare.

• Customs and Practices: "Indica" included information about contemporary customs, diets, festivals, and religious practices, and reported that India had no slavery.

• Megasthenes also provided an account of Chandragupta Maurya’s reign and wrote about the prosperity and peace within the empire.

• It is important to note that "Indica" had some inaccuracies or exaggerations possibly due to misunderstandings or cultural differences. For example, Megasthenes reported on creatures such as giant ants that dug up gold dust and humans with no mouths, which are widely considered to be based on misunderstandings or myths.

q:
The question consists of two statements, namely, Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Use them to choose the correct alternative.

Assertion (A): During the British rule, India’s exports exceeded the imports leading to surplus of balance of trade.

Reason (R): The surplus of balance of trade was used for growth and development of India.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
A is true and R is false
solution:
The correct answer is A is true and R is false.

Key Points

Explanation:

Assertion (A): India did indeed have a surplus in its balance of trade during most of the British Raj.

• This means that the value of its exports exceeded the value of its imports.

• This was due to several factors, including:

• Forced cultivation of cash crops: The British forced Indian farmers to grow crops like indigo and cotton for export, even if it meant neglecting food production for domestic consumption.

• Deindustrialization: British policies destroyed India's traditional industries, making the country more dependent on imported manufactured goods.

• Drain of wealth: A significant portion of the trade surplus was not reinvested in India, but sent back to Britain as tribute and profits for British companies.

Reason (R): However, the statement that the surplus of the balance of trade was used for the growth and development of India is false.

• The benefits of the trade surplus primarily accrued to the British, while India suffered from:

• Underdevelopment: The drain of wealth and focus on cash crops over food production stunted India's economic development and exacerbated poverty.

• Exploitation: Indian farmers and laborers were often exploited by British companies and landowners, receiving meager wages and working in poor conditions.

• Lack of infrastructure: Despite the trade surplus, the British invested very little in India's infrastructure, such as roads, railways, and education, which further hampered development.

Therefore, while it is true that India had a positive balance of trade under British rule, the surplus was not used for its growth and development, but rather benefited the British at the expense of the Indian people.

q: According to which of the following foreign travellers, people of Delhi used to write letters containing abuses to the Sultan, therefore, in order to punish them Sultan decided to shift the capital?

• Ibn Batuta visited India during the reign of Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

• According to his accounts, the people of Delhi used to write letters containing abuses to the Sultan.

• To punish them, the Sultan decided to shift the capital from Delhi to Devagiri, which he renamed as Daulatabad.

• Hasan Nizami:

• He is best known for his historical work "Futuh al-Salatin" (The Conquests of Kings), which provides an account of the history of the Delhi Sultanate.

• His work is a valuable source for understanding the history of medieval India, particularly during the reign of the early Sultans

q: Who among the following was the last sultan of Delhi sultanate?
solution:
The correct answer is Ibrahim Lodi.

Key Points

• Ibrahim Lodi was the last ruler of the Delhi Sultanate from the Lodi dynasty.

• He reigned from 1517 until his defeat and death in the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.

• Ibrahim Lodi was the son of Sikandar Lodi and ascended to the throne after his father's death.

• His rule marked the end of the Delhi Sultanate and the beginning of the Mughal Empire in India.

Additional Information

• Delhi Sultanate

• The Delhi Sultanate was a Muslim kingdom that ruled over large parts of the Indian subcontinent for over 300 years, from 1206 to 1526.

• It was established by Qutb-ud-din Aibak after the defeat of Prithviraj Chauhan and marked the beginning of Muslim rule in India.

• The Sultanate saw the rise and fall of several dynasties including the Mamluks, Khaljis, Tughlaqs, Sayyids, and Lodis.

• It played a crucial role in shaping the culture, architecture, and administration of India during the medieval period.

• First Battle of Panipat

• The First Battle of Panipat was fought on April 21, 1526, between the forces of the Mughal ruler Babur and the Lodi dynasty's Sultan Ibrahim Lodi.

• The battle marked the end of the Delhi Sultanate and the beginning of the Mughal Empire in India.

• Babur's use of innovative military tactics and artillery was instrumental in his victory.

• This battle is considered one of the most significant events in Indian history as it led to the establishment of Mughal rule, which lasted for over three centuries.

• Mughal Empire

• The Mughal Empire was an empire that controlled large parts of the Indian subcontinent from the early 16th to the mid-19th century.

• It was founded by Babur, a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, after his victory in the First Battle of Panipat.

• The Mughal Empire is known for its rich cultural contributions, including significant developments in art, architecture, and cuisine.

• Some of the most famous Mughal rulers include Akbar, Shah Jahan, and Aurangzeb.

q: Who among the following was one of the Navratnas of Akbar?
solution:
The correct answer is Tansen.

Key Points

• Tansen was one of the nine jewels (Navratnas) in the court of Emperor Akbar.

• He was a prominent figure in North Indian classical music and is known for his contributions to Hindustani music.

• Tansen's real name was Ramtanu Pandey, and he was born in a Hindu Gaur Brahmin family in Gwalior.

• He is credited with creating several ragas, including raga Darbari Kanada, raga Miyan ki Todi, and raga Miyan ki Malhar.

Additional Information

• Navratnas

• The term "Navratnas" refers to the nine extraordinary people in the court of Emperor Akbar who were known for their exceptional abilities and expertise in various fields.

• The Navratnas included scholars, poets, musicians, and advisors who played significant roles in Akbar's administration and cultural life.

• Besides Tansen, the other Navratnas were Abul Fazl, Faizi, Raja Todar Mal, Raja Man Singh, Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khana, Fakir Aziao-Din, Mullah Do Piaza, and Raja Birbal.

• Each of these individuals was recognized for their unique contributions to the Mughal court and the broader Indian cultural landscape.

• Hindustani Classical Music

• Hindustani classical music is one of the two main subgenres of Indian classical music, the other being Carnatic music.

• It originated in the northern regions of the Indian subcontinent and has a rich tradition of ragas and talas.

• It emphasizes improvisation and the exploration of the raga, a framework for melodic improvisation.

• Tansen is considered one of the greatest musicians in Hindustani classical music and has left a lasting impact on its development.

q: Valabhi, a city of ancient India was the capital of the _ dynasty from the 5th to 8th Century CE.
solution:
The correct answer is Maitraka.

Key Points

• The Maitraka dynasty ruled in the western part of India, primarily the region of present-day Gujarat.

• Valabhi, the capital city of the Maitraka dynasty, was an important cultural and educational center during their reign.

• The dynasty was founded by Senapati Bhatarka, a former Gupta Empire military commander, around the middle of the 5th century CE.

• The Maitrakas were patrons of Buddhism and Jainism, and Valabhi was known for its Buddhist monasteries and Jain temples.

Additional Information

• Valabhi

• Valabhi was an ancient city located in the present-day Bhavnagar district of Gujarat, India.

• It served as the capital of the Maitraka dynasty from the 5th to the 8th century CE.

• Valabhi was renowned as a center of learning and attracted scholars from various parts of India.

• The city was known for its educational institutions, particularly Buddhist monasteries, which were comparable to those at Nalanda.

• Maitraka Dynasty

• The Maitraka dynasty was founded by Senapati Bhatarka, a former military governor of the Gupta Empire.

• They ruled primarily over the Saurashtra region of Gujarat from the 5th to the 8th century CE.

• The Maitrakas played a significant role in the cultural and religious development of western India.

• The dynasty came to an end in the mid-8th century CE, likely due to Arab invasions and internal strife.

• Gupta Empire

• The Gupta Empire was an ancient Indian empire that existed from approximately 320 to 550 CE.

• Founded by Maharaja Sri Gupta, the empire is known for its achievements in the arts, architecture, sciences, religion, and philosophy.

• The period of the Gupta Empire is often referred to as the Golden Age of India due to the extensive cultural developments and prosperity.

• The Gupta rulers supported Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism, fostering a diverse cultural and religious landscape.

• Buddhism and Jainism

• Buddhism is a major world religion founded by Siddhartha Gautama, known as the Buddha, in the 5th century BCE in India.

• Buddhism emphasizes the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path as a way to achieve enlightenment and end suffering.

• Jainism is an ancient Indian religion that teaches non-violence, truth, and asceticism.

• Founded by Mahavira in the 6th century BCE, Jainism emphasizes the principles of non-attachment and self-discipline.

q: Which of the following battles is considered the formal beginning of the British Raj in India?
solution:
The correct answer is Battle of Plassey.

Key Points

• The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757, in the eastern part of India.

• This battle marked the beginning of British colonial rule in India.

• It was fought between the British East India Company and the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj ud-Daulah.

• The British victory in this battle was largely due to the betrayal of Nawab's commander, Mir Jafar, who sided with the British.

Additional Information

• First Carnatic War

• The First Carnatic War (1746-1748) was fought between the British and the French in India.

• It was mainly a result of the War of Austrian Succession in Europe.

• The war ended with the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1748, resulting in a status quo ante bellum.

• Battle of Wandiwash

• The Battle of Wandiwash was fought on 22 January 1760 between the British and the French.

• The British, under Sir Eyre Coote, decisively defeated the French forces.

• This battle marked the end of French colonial ambitions in India.

• Battle of Buxar

• The Battle of Buxar was fought on 22 October 1764 between the British East India Company and the combined forces of the Nawab of Bengal, Nawab of Awadh, and the Mughal Emperor.

• The British victory established their supremacy in the eastern parts of India.

• This battle was crucial for the British as it consolidated their power after the Battle of Plassey.

q: Which party formed the government in Britain in the year 1945?
solution:
The correct answer is Labour Party.

Key Points

• In the 1945 general election, the Labour Party won a landslide victory, securing 393 seats out of 640.

• This election marked a significant turning point in British political history, with the Labour Party forming its first majority government.

• The Labour Party, led by Clement Attlee, implemented numerous social reforms, including the establishment of the National Health Service (NHS).

• The 1945 election is often seen as a mandate for post-war reconstruction and the creation of a welfare state.

Additional Information

• Labour Party

• The Labour Party is a centre-left political party in the United Kingdom.

• It was founded in 1900, growing out of the trade union movement and socialist parties of the 19th century.

• The party's platform has historically included policies aimed at reducing inequality and promoting social welfare.

• The Labour Party's 1945 victory is often credited to its promises of widespread social reform and economic recovery following World War II.

• Clement Attlee

• He was the leader of the Labour Party from 1935 to 1955 and served as Prime Minister from 1945 to 1951.

• Attlee's government is known for nationalizing major industries and public utilities and establishing the NHS.

• Under his leadership, the Labour government implemented extensive social reforms, laying the foundations for the modern British welfare state.

• National Health Service (NHS)

• The NHS was established in 1948, providing healthcare to all UK residents based on need rather than the ability to pay.

• It was one of the major social reforms introduced by the post-1945 Labour government.

• The creation of the NHS is considered one of the Labour Party's most significant achievements.

• 1945 General Election

• The election was held on 5 July 1945, with the results declared on 26 July after votes from servicemen overseas were counted.

• It was the first general election to be held in Britain since 1935, as elections had been suspended during World War II.

• The Labour Party's victory ended nearly a decade of Conservative government under Winston Churchill.

q: In which of the following cities did Mahatma Gandhi lead the peasant movement against the imposed indigo cultivation by the British planters?
solution:
The correct answer is Champaran.

Key Points

• Champaran is famous for the Champaran Satyagraha of 1917 where Mahatma Gandhi led a movement against the British planters who forced local farmers to grow indigo under harsh conditions.

• This movement marked Gandhi's first active involvement in the Indian freedom struggle and was a significant milestone in India's path to independence.

• The success of the Champaran movement brought Gandhi to the forefront of the Indian independence movement.

• The indigo planters in Champaran were exploiting the farmers by forcing them to grow indigo on a portion of their land and sell it at fixed prices, which was economically detrimental to the farmers.

Additional Information

• Mahatma Gandhi

• Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, popularly known as Mahatma Gandhi, was a prominent leader of the Indian independence movement against British rule.

• He is known for his philosophy of non-violence (Ahimsa) and civil disobedience, which he employed to lead India to independence.

• Gandhi's methods inspired movements for civil rights and freedom across the world.

• He is often referred to as the "Father of the Nation" in India for his pivotal role in the country's struggle for independence.

• Indigo Cultivation

• Indigo was a valuable dye in the textile industry during the colonial period.

• British planters in India forced local farmers to grow indigo under the Tinkathia system, where farmers had to grow indigo on 3/20th (or roughly 15%) of their land.

• This system was highly exploitative as the indigo crop depleted the soil, and the farmers received very low prices for their produce.

• The Champaran Satyagraha was a protest against this system and highlighted the plight of the farmers.

• Satyagraha

• Satyagraha is a form of nonviolent resistance or civil resistance.

• The term was coined and developed by Mahatma Gandhi during the Indian independence movement.

• Satyagraha is based on the principle of nonviolence and seeks to bring about social and political change through passive resistance and peaceful protests.

• It emphasizes the power of truth and the need to adhere to ethical principles in the face of injustice.

q: Which of the following organisations, divided into two branches, was established by Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Annie Besant?
solution:

• The Home Rule League was a national political organization in India that aimed to achieve self-government within the British Empire.

• It was established by Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Annie Besant in 1916.

• The organization was divided into two branches: Tilak's Home Rule League (based in Maharashtra) and Besant's Home Rule League (based in Madras).

• The leagues were influential in mobilizing Indian public opinion and educating the masses on self-rule and nationalistic ideas.

• The Indian Association was founded by Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose in 1876.

• It aimed to promote political education and rights among Indians and was a precursor to the Indian National Congress.

• Theosophical Society

• The Theosophical Society was founded by Helena Petrovna Blavatsky, Henry Steel Olcott, and others in 1875 in New York City.

• Annie Besant was a prominent member who later became its president and played a significant role in India's independence movement.

• The East Indian Association was founded by Dadabhai Naoroji in 1866 in London.

• It aimed to promote Indian interests and create a platform for Indian grievances in the UK.

• Home Rule League

• The Home Rule League was a movement that sought self-government for India within the British Empire.

• It drew inspiration from the Irish Home Rule Movement and was a significant milestone in India's struggle for independence.

q: The Vedangas are Hindu auxiliary disciplines that originated in ancient times and are linked to the study of the Vedas. These are _ in number.
solution:
The correct answer is six.

Key Points

• The Vedangas are six auxiliary disciplines associated with the study of the Vedas.

• They were developed in ancient India to support the proper understanding and interpretation of the Vedas.

• The six Vedangas are: Shiksha (Phonetics), Vyakarana (Grammar), Chandas (Meter), Nirukta (Etymology), Jyotisha (Astronomy), and Kalpa (Rituals).

• Each Vedanga serves a specific purpose in ensuring the accurate preservation, recitation, and understanding of the Vedic texts.

Additional Information

• Shiksha (Phonetics)

• Shiksha deals with the sounds of the Sanskrit language, including the rules of pronunciation, accent, and intonation.

• It is essential for maintaining the oral tradition of the Vedas by ensuring accurate and consistent recitation.

• Vyakarana (Grammar)

• Vyakarana is the study of Sanskrit grammar and linguistic analysis.

• The most famous text of Vyakarana is Panini's Ashtadhyayi, which codifies the rules of Sanskrit grammar.

• Chandas (Metrics)

• Chandas is the study of poetic meters used in Vedic texts.

• It helps in understanding the structure and rhythmic patterns of Vedic hymns.

• Nirukta (Etymology)

• Nirukta involves the interpretation and explanation of difficult Vedic words.

• Yaska's Nirukta is a significant work in this field, providing meanings and contexts of Vedic terms.

• Jyotisha (Astronomy)

• Jyotisha is the study of astronomy and astrology as related to Vedic rituals.

• It includes the calculation of auspicious times (muhurta) for performing Vedic rituals.

• Kalpa (Rituals)

• Kalpa deals with the procedures and rituals of Vedic ceremonies.

• It includes various texts like the Shrauta Sutras, Grihya Sutras, and Dharma Sutras, which guide the performance of Vedic rituals.

q: In which of the following battles did Muhammad of Ghor defeat Jayachandra of Gahadavala dynasty in 1194 AD?

q: Who established Shantiniketan and when?
solution:
The correct answer is Ravindranath Tagore, 1901.

• Rabindranath Tagore established Shantiniketan as an experimental school aimed at blending the best of Western and Indian educational systems.

• He is often referred to as the "Bard of Bengal" and is best known for his poetry and songs, including the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.

• The university is located in Shantiniketan, West Bengal, and is known for its unique approach to education, emphasizing the harmony between man and nature.

• It offers a wide range of programs in humanities, social sciences, science, music, fine arts, and performing arts.

• Visva-Bharati continues to attract students and scholars from around the world, maintaining its legacy as a place of cultural and intellectual exchange.

• Shantiniketan, meaning "Abode of Peace", was originally an ashram built by Rabindranath Tagore's father, Maharshi Devendranath Tagore.

• Rabindranath Tagore expanded Shantiniketan into an experimental school with an emphasis on natural surroundings, creativity, and learning through exploration.

• Shantiniketan later evolved into Visva-Bharati University, becoming a prominent center for education and cultural activities.

• The place remains a symbol of Tagore's vision of a holistic and inclusive education system.

q: Who among the following is primarily connected to the World’s Parliament of Religions convened in Chicago, 1893?

• The aim of the INA was to secure Indian independence from British rule, a cause that garnered significant support among Indian expatriates and prisoners of war.

• Mohan Singh initially formed the INA with Indian prisoners of war captured by the Japanese during the Malayan Campaign and the Battle of Singapore.

• Subhas Chandra Bose, a prominent leader in the Indian independence movement, took charge of the INA in 1943 and restructured it significantly.

• Subhas Chandra Bose

• Subhas Chandra Bose, also known as Netaji, was a prominent Indian freedom fighter who played a crucial role in the Indian independence movement.

• Bose was a charismatic leader who advocated for radical action against British rule and sought foreign alliances to achieve Indian independence.

• Under his leadership, the INA sought to liberate India from British control with the assistance of the Axis powers during World War II.

• Bose's efforts and his call for complete independence inspired many Indians and left a lasting legacy in India's history.

• World War II and Southeast Asia

• World War II, which lasted from 1939 to 1945, involved major global powers and was marked by significant military campaigns in various regions, including Southeast Asia.

• Southeast Asia was strategically important during the war, with countries like Singapore, Malaya, and Burma witnessing major battles.

• The Japanese occupation of Southeast Asia during the war provided an opportunity for Indian nationalists to seek support for their cause against British colonial rule.

• The INA's formation and activities in Southeast Asia were part of the broader context of anti-colonial struggles and the global impact of World War II.

q: The Maukharis ruled over which of the following cities in western Uttar Pradesh that over the time replaced Pataliputra as a political centre of north India?
solution:
The correct answer is Kannauj.

Key Points

• Kannauj, located in western Uttar Pradesh, was an ancient city and a significant political center in northern India.

• The Maukharis were a dynasty that ruled over Kannauj before it became a prominent city under the later rulers such as the Gurjara-Pratiharas.

• Over time, Kannauj replaced Pataliputra (modern-day Patna) as the political and cultural center of northern India.

• Kannauj is known for its historical significance and its strategic location which made it a focal point of power struggles among various dynasties.

Additional Information

• Maukharis Dynasty:

• The Maukharis were a dynasty that ruled parts of northern India during the early medieval period, roughly between the 6th and 7th centuries.

• They initially served as vassals of the Gupta Empire but later established their independence.

• The most notable ruler of the Maukharis was Isanavarman, who expanded their territory and consolidated power.

• The Maukhari dynasty is known for its contribution to the political and cultural landscape of northern India during its time.

• Kannauj:

• Kannauj, also known as Kanyakubja, has a rich history dating back to ancient times.

• It was a major center of trade, culture, and politics and remained so through various dynasties, including the Maukharis, Harshavardhana, and the Gurjara-Pratiharas.

• Kannauj is famously known for its production of perfumes and essential oils, particularly the traditional "attar" (perfume).

• Throughout its history, Kannauj has been a coveted city, leading to numerous battles and power struggles among regional powers.

• Pataliputra:

• Pataliputra, modern-day Patna, was the capital city of several ancient Indian empires, including the Maurya and Gupta Empires.

• It was a major political, economic, and cultural hub during its peak.

• Over time, the political center shifted from Pataliputra to other cities like Kannauj as different dynasties rose to power.

• Pataliputra is historically significant for its role in the administration and governance of ancient Indian empires.

q: An inscription, Takht-i-Bahi recovered from Mardan near Peshawar, indicates the rule of which of the following dynasties in north-western area of present Pakistan?
solution:
The correct answer is Parthians.

Key Points

• The Parthian Empire ruled over a significant part of ancient Iran and extended their domain into the northwestern regions of the Indian subcontinent, including parts of present-day Pakistan.

• The Parthian period is known for its cultural syncretism, blending Greek, Persian, and regional influences, which is reflected in their art, architecture, and inscriptions.

• Takht-i-Bahi, a historical site near Mardan in present-day Pakistan, is famous for its Buddhist monastery ruins, which flourished during the Parthian period.

• The Parthian rulers in this region were known for their patronage of Buddhism, which contributed to the spread and development of Buddhist culture and architecture.

Additional Information

• Takht-i-Bahi

• Takht-i-Bahi is an archaeological site of an ancient Buddhist monastery situated in Mardan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan.

• The site is renowned for its well-preserved ruins, which date back to the 1st century CE and were in use until the 7th century CE.

• The name "Takht-i-Bahi" means "Throne of the Water Spring" in Persian, indicating the presence of a spring near the monastery.

• The monastery complex includes stupas, courtyards, meditation cells, and assembly halls, reflecting the architectural style and cultural influences of the Parthian period.

• Parthian Empire

• The Parthian Empire, also known as the Arsacid Empire, was a major Iranian political and cultural power in ancient Persia, which lasted from approximately 247 BCE to 224 CE.

• The Parthians were known for their unique style of governance, which combined elements of Greek, Persian, and regional traditions.

• Their empire stretched from the Euphrates River in the west to the Indus River in the east, including regions of modern-day Iran, Iraq, Armenia, and parts of Pakistan and Afghanistan.

• Parthian art, architecture, and inscriptions, including those found at sites like Takht-i-Bahi, reflect a blend of Hellenistic and Persian influences.

• Sakas

• The Sakas, also known as the Scythians, were a group of ancient Iranian nomadic tribes who migrated into the Indian subcontinent during the 1st century BCE.

• They established several kingdoms in the northwestern regions of India, including the Indo-Scythian kingdom.

• The Sakas were known for their contributions to the cultural and political landscape of ancient India, including the development of the Saka era calendar.

• Indo-Greek Kingdom

• The Indo-Greek Kingdom was established by Greek rulers who invaded and settled in the northwestern regions of the Indian subcontinent during the 2nd century BCE.

• The Indo-Greek rulers are known for their coinage, which often featured a blend of Greek and Indian artistic styles and inscriptions.

• Their rule contributed to the spread of Hellenistic culture and the fusion of Greek and Indian cultural elements in art, architecture, and religion.

q: Deimachus who was a Greek ambassador came to India during the reign of the Mauryan king, .
solution:
The correct answer is Bindusara.

Key Points

• Deimachus was a Greek ambassador who came to India during the reign of the Mauryan king Bindusara.

• Bindusara was the second Mauryan emperor, ruling from c. 297 to c. 273 BCE.

• He was the son of Chandragupta Maurya, the founder of the Maurya Dynasty.

• Bindusara maintained diplomatic relations with various Hellenistic states, including the Seleucid Empire.

Additional Information

• Bindusara

• Bindusara, also known as Amitraghata, was the second emperor of the Mauryan dynasty.

• He succeeded his father, Chandragupta Maurya, and ruled from c. 297 BCE to c. 273 BCE.

• Bindusara is known for his administrative skills and the expansion of the Mauryan Empire.

• He maintained friendly relations with the Hellenistic kingdoms, which were established by the successors of Alexander the Great.

• Deimachus

• Deimachus was a Greek envoy sent by Antiochus I, the Seleucid king, to the Mauryan court.

• His visit to India is recorded as part of the diplomatic relations between the Mauryan Empire and the Hellenistic world.

• Deimachus succeeded Megasthenes, another Greek ambassador, at the Mauryan court.

• Mauryan Empire

• The Mauryan Empire was the first large-scale empire in India, founded by Chandragupta Maurya in 322 BCE.

• It is known for its significant achievements in political, military, and cultural fields.

• The empire reached its zenith under Ashoka the Great, who is renowned for his promotion of Buddhism and non-violence.

• Diplomatic Relations

• During the Mauryan period, diplomatic relations were established with several Hellenistic kingdoms, including the Seleucid Empire.

• These relations were crucial for trade, cultural exchange, and political alliances.

• Greek ambassadors like Megasthenes and Deimachus played a key role in these diplomatic efforts.

q: Who among the following rulers built five astronomical observatories at different places in north India?
solution:
The correct answer is Sawai Jaisingh II.

Key Points

• Sawai Jaisingh II was a notable ruler of the Amber kingdom in the early 18th century.

• He built five astronomical observatories, known as Jantar Mantar, located in Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura, and Varanasi.

• The primary purpose of these observatories was to study the movements of celestial bodies and predict astronomical events.

• These observatories are significant examples of Indian scientific heritage and architectural ingenuity.

Additional Information

• Sawai Jaisingh II

• He was the ruler of Amber (later Jaipur) from 1699 to 1743.

• Jaisingh was a scholar in astronomy, mathematics, and architecture. He was deeply interested in the study of celestial bodies.

• His observatories combined elements of Mughal architecture with traditional Indian styles, reflecting his innovative approach.

• The observatories were equipped with large instruments made of stone and brass, designed for precise astronomical measurements.

• Jantar Mantar Observatories

• These are collections of architectural astronomical instruments, built in the early 18th century.

• The largest of these observatories is located in Jaipur, which also serves as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

• The instruments at Jantar Mantar were designed to observe and measure the positions of stars, predict eclipses, and ascertain the declinations of celestial bodies.

• The observatories are a testament to the advanced scientific knowledge and architectural prowess of that era.

• Historical Context

• During the rule of Sawai Jaisingh II, there was significant cultural and scientific exchange between India and other parts of the world.

• Jaisingh's patronage of science and architecture led to advancements in various fields, including astronomy, which was crucial for navigation and timekeeping.

• The construction of the Jantar Mantar observatories marked a significant period in the history of Indian science and demonstrated the ruler's commitment to knowledge and innovation.

q: Who among the following was the successor of Mughal Emperor, Babur?
solution:
The correct answer is Humayun.

Key Points

• Humayun was the son of Babur, the founder of the Mughal Empire in India.

• Humayun succeeded his father Babur after his death in 1530.

• Humayun's reign was marked by a series of setbacks and recoveries, including being ousted from his kingdom by Sher Shah Suri.

• He eventually regained his throne with the help of the Persian Empire and re-established Mughal rule in India before his accidental death in 1556.

Additional Information

• Babur

• Babur was the founder of the Mughal Empire in India, establishing it after his victory at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.

• He was a descendant of Timur on his father's side and Genghis Khan on his mother's side.

• Babur's contributions laid the foundation for a powerful and enduring empire in the Indian subcontinent.

• Humayun

• Humayun was the eldest son of Babur and succeeded him as the second Mughal Emperor.

• His full name was Nasir-ud-Din Muḥammad Humayun.

• Humayun faced challenges from Afghan and Rajput rulers and was defeated by Sher Shah Suri, leading to his temporary exile.

• With Persian assistance, Humayun was able to reclaim his throne in 1555.

• Sher Shah Suri

• Sher Shah Suri was an Afghan ruler who defeated Humayun and established the Suri Empire in India.

• He is known for his administrative reforms, including the introduction of the Rupiya and the improvement of infrastructure.

• Sher Shah's rule was short-lived, but his policies greatly influenced the Mughal administration.

• Mughal Empire

• The Mughal Empire was a prominent empire in the Indian subcontinent that lasted from the early 16th to the mid-18th century.

• It was known for its rich cultural contributions, monumental architecture, and the amalgamation of Persian and Indian cultures.

• The empire reached its zenith under rulers like Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, and Aurangzeb.

q: Under which of the following Pala king's patronage the Vikramshila university in 8th century India was founded?
solution:
The correct answer is Dharmapala.

Key Points

• Dharmapala was a prominent ruler of the Pala dynasty in ancient India.

• He ruled during the 8th century and is known for his significant contributions to education and Buddhism.

• Under his patronage, the Vikramshila University was established to promote Buddhist learning and scholarship.

• Dharmapala's reign marked the height of the Pala Empire's influence and cultural achievements.

Additional Information

• Pala Dynasty

• The Pala Dynasty ruled parts of Bengal and Bihar in the Indian subcontinent from the 8th to the 12th century.

• The dynasty was founded by Gopala in the mid-8th century.

• The Palas were known for their patronage of Buddhism and their support for educational institutions.

• They built several monasteries and universities, including Nalanda and Vikramshila.

• Vikramshila University

• Vikramshila University was one of the most important centers of Buddhist learning in ancient India.

• It was established by Dharmapala around the late 8th or early 9th century.

• The university attracted scholars from all over Asia, including Tibet, China, and Southeast Asia.

• It specialized in various fields of knowledge, including philosophy, logic, grammar, and metaphysics.

• Buddhist Learning

• During the Pala period, Buddhism flourished in India, and several monasteries and universities were established to promote its teachings.

• These institutions became centers of learning and attracted students from different parts of the world.

• They played a crucial role in the preservation and dissemination of Buddhist texts and teachings.

q: Which of the following animals was the emblem of the Chola dynasty?
solution:
The correct answer is Tiger.

Key Points

• The tiger was the emblem of the Chola dynasty, which was one of the longest-ruling dynasties in the history of southern India.

• The Chola dynasty used the tiger emblem to symbolize their strength, courage, and dominance over their territory.

• The emblem can be found on many of the Chola inscriptions, coins, and temple walls, indicating its importance as a royal insignia.

• The tiger emblem not only represented the power of the Chola kings but also their commitment to protecting their kingdom and upholding justice.

Additional Information

• Chola Dynasty

• The Chola dynasty was a Tamil dynasty that ruled primarily in southern India until the 13th century.

• Tiger Emblem

• The tiger symbol was chosen by the Cholas to reflect their royal and warrior status.

• The emblem is often depicted in various artistic forms, such as sculptures and carvings, in the temples built by the Chola rulers.

• It served as a unifying symbol for the Chola empire, representing the courage and valor of its people.

• Historical artifacts like coins and inscriptions bearing the tiger emblem provide insights into the cultural and political landscape of the Chola period.

• Influence of the Cholas

• The Cholas played a pivotal role in the spread of Hinduism and the construction of grand temples, such as the Brihadeeswarar Temple in Thanjavur.

• Their naval prowess helped in establishing maritime trade routes with Southeast Asia, contributing to the cultural exchange and economic prosperity of the region.

• The Chola administration is noted for its efficient governance, including the development of a systematic revenue collection mechanism.

• Their patronage of art and architecture left a lasting legacy that continues to be admired and studied for its grandeur and sophistication.

q: Wood’s Dispatch of 1854 primarily dealt with which of the following subject matters?
solution:
The correct answer is Education.

Key Points

• Wood's Dispatch of 1854 is considered the Magna Carta of English Education in India.

• The Dispatch recommended a system of education from the primary level to the university level.

• It proposed the establishment of universities in major cities like Bombay, Calcutta, and Madras.

• Wood's Dispatch emphasized the need for vocational and female education.

Additional Information

• Wood's Dispatch

• Wood's Dispatch was a comprehensive plan for the education system in India, formulated by Sir Charles Wood, the President of the Board of Control of the British East India Company, in 1854.

• It laid the foundation for a systematic and organized education policy in India under British rule.

• The Dispatch recommended the establishment of a Department of Public Instruction in each province to oversee education matters.

• It also suggested the use of vernacular languages at the primary level, while English was to be the medium of instruction for higher education.

• Universities in Major Cities

• Following the recommendations of Wood's Dispatch, universities were established in Bombay, Calcutta, and Madras in 1857.

• These universities played a crucial role in shaping modern education in India and produced many notable scholars and leaders.

• Vocational and Female Education

• Wood's Dispatch emphasized the importance of vocational education to improve the skills of the workforce.

• It also highlighted the need for female education to uplift the status of women in society.

• Special grants were recommended to promote female education.

q: Who among the following founded the Atmiya Sabha in 1814?
solution:
The correct answer is Raja Rammohun Roy.

Key Points

• Raja Rammohun Roy was a prominent social and educational reformer in India during the early 19th century.

• He founded the Atmiya Sabha in 1814, which later became the Brahmo Samaj, to promote social and religious reforms.

• The Atmiya Sabha was established to fight against the social evils such as caste discrimination, and to promote monotheism and rational thinking.

• Rammohun Roy is often called the "Father of the Indian Renaissance" for his efforts to modernize Indian society.

Additional Information

• Raja Rammohun Roy:

• Born on May 22, 1772, in Radhanagar, Bengal, Rammohun Roy was a pioneer in the Indian social reform movement.

• He opposed practices such as sati (the burning of widows), child marriage, and caste discrimination, advocating for women's rights and education.

• Rammohun Roy was also instrumental in the establishment of the Hindu College in Calcutta in 1817, which later became Presidency College.

• His efforts in advocating for the abolition of sati led to the regulation banning the practice in 1829 by the British Governor-General, Lord William Bentinck.

• Atmiya Sabha:

• Founded in 1814, the Atmiya Sabha was an organization that aimed to discuss and propagate the ideas of monotheism and rationality.

• The Sabha's meetings involved discussions on the Upanishads, Vedas, and other scriptures to interpret them in a way that promoted a monotheistic view.

• It served as a platform for intellectuals to debate and discuss various social issues and the need for reforms in Hindu society.

• The Atmiya Sabha's activities laid the foundation for the later establishment of the Brahmo Samaj in 1828, which continued the reformist agenda.

• Brahmo Samaj:

• Founded by Raja Rammohun Roy in 1828, the Brahmo Samaj was a socio-religious reform movement that aimed to purify Hinduism and promote monotheism.

• The Brahmo Samaj sought to eliminate social evils such as caste discrimination, child marriage, and the dowry system.

• It emphasized the importance of education, especially for women, and supported widow remarriage.

• The movement had a significant impact on the Indian society and influenced many later reformers and movements.

• Social Reform in India:

• The early 19th century saw the emergence of several social reform movements in India aimed at addressing various social issues and promoting modernization.

• Reformers like Raja Rammohun Roy, Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, and Swami Vivekananda played crucial roles in advocating for change and improving the status of women and marginalized communities.

• These movements laid the groundwork for future social and political developments in India, including the struggle for independence.

• The reforms also contributed to the development of a more progressive and inclusive society in India.

q: Samata Sainik Dal was formed in 1927 by whom among the following personalities?
solution:
The correct answer is BR Ambedkar.

Key Points

• BR Ambedkar, also known as Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar, was a prominent Indian jurist, economist, politician, and social reformer.

• He is best known for his efforts in fighting for the rights of the Dalits (formerly known as untouchables) and other socially backward classes in India.

• He played a key role in the drafting of the Indian Constitution and served as the first Law and Justice Minister of independent India.

• The Samata Sainik Dal, formed in 1927, was an organization aimed at providing protection and promoting the social and political rights of the oppressed classes in India.

Additional Information

• Savitribai Phule

• She was an Indian social reformer, educationalist, and poet from Maharashtra.

• She is regarded as the first female teacher in India and played a crucial role in improving women's rights in the country.

• Along with her husband Jyotirao Phule, she founded the first girls' school in Pune in 1848.

• Mahatma Gandhi

• He was an Indian lawyer, anti-colonial nationalist, and political ethicist.

• He employed nonviolent resistance to lead the successful campaign for India's independence from British rule.

• He is internationally recognized for his philosophy of Satyagraha (truth and nonviolent resistance).

• Narayana Guru

• He was a social reformer and spiritual leader from Kerala.

• He led a reform movement against the caste system in the Hindu society.

• He emphasized the significance of education, spirituality, and social equality in the upliftment of the downtrodden sections of society.

q: In the second Round Table Conference, Mahatma Gandhi represented which of the following parties?
solution:
The correct answer is Indian National Congress.

Key Points

• Mahatma Gandhi, a pivotal leader in the Indian independence movement, represented the Indian National Congress at the Second Round Table Conference.

• The Second Round Table Conference was held in London from September 7, 1931, to December 1, 1931.

• The Indian National Congress was a major political party in India that aimed to gain independence from British rule.

• Gandhi attended the conference to present the demands and aspirations of the Indian people and to negotiate for the country's independence.

Additional Information

• Round Table Conferences

• The Round Table Conferences were a series of three conferences organized by the British government to discuss constitutional reforms in India.

• The first conference was held in London from November 1930 to January 1931, the second from September to December 1931, and the third from November to December 1932.

• The conferences were attended by representatives of various Indian political parties, princely states, and British officials.

• The aim was to formulate plans for the future governance of India and address the demands of Indian leaders for greater self-rule.

• Indian National Congress

• The Indian National Congress (INC) was founded in 1885 and played a significant role in the Indian independence movement.

• It was the principal party that led the struggle against British colonial rule and advocated for the rights and self-governance of Indians.

• Key leaders included Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, and many others who contributed to India's fight for independence.

• The INC adopted various methods of protest, including non-violent civil disobedience, boycotts, and mass movements to challenge British policies.

• Mahatma Gandhi

• Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, popularly known as Mahatma Gandhi, was a prominent leader in the Indian independence movement.

• He is best known for his philosophy of non-violence (Ahimsa) and civil disobedience (Satyagraha).

• Gandhi's leadership and methods inspired millions of Indians to participate in the freedom struggle through peaceful means.

• His efforts played a crucial role in India achieving independence from British rule on August 15, 1947.

q: British Parliament introduced Indian High Courts Act in which year?
solution:
The correct answer is 1861.

Key Points

• The Indian High Courts Act was introduced by the British Parliament in the year 1861.

• This act led to the establishment of High Courts in India for the first time, replacing the older Supreme Courts at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.

• The High Courts were given extensive original and appellate jurisdiction, marking a significant shift in the Indian judicial system.

• These High Courts were modeled after the English judicial system and were intended to provide a higher level of judicial administration in the major cities of India.

Additional Information

• Indian High Courts Act 1861

• The Indian High Courts Act 1861 was an act of the British Parliament that led to the creation of High Courts in India in the three Presidency towns of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.

• Before this act, the judicial system in these cities was managed by Supreme Courts, which were established under the Charter Act of 1774.

• The new High Courts were granted original civil and criminal jurisdiction, appellate jurisdiction, and supervisory jurisdiction over the lower courts.

• This act was significant as it brought uniformity and improvement in the judicial administration of British India.

• Supreme Courts of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras

• These courts were established under the Regulating Act of 1773 and subsequent acts, and they functioned until the High Courts were established in 1861.

• They were the highest courts in British India and had both original and appellate jurisdiction.

• The Supreme Courts were replaced by the High Courts to streamline and improve the judicial system.

• Judicial Administration in British India

• The British introduced several reforms to the judicial system in India to make it more efficient and aligned with British legal principles.

• The High Courts Act was a part of these reforms, which aimed to enhance the administration of justice in the colonies.

• These reforms were crucial in shaping the modern Indian judicial system.

q: The Pandya Kingdom was first mentioned by Megasthenes, who said that their kingdom was famous for pearls. Their capital was:
solution:
The correct answer is Madurai.

Key Points

• Madurai was the capital of the ancient Pandya Kingdom, known for its flourishing trade and cultural heritage.

• The city is famous for the Meenakshi Amman Temple, a historic Hindu temple located on the southern bank of the Vaigai River.

• It has been a major settlement for two millennia and is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.

• Madurai has a rich historical background and has been mentioned in ancient texts and inscriptions, highlighting its significance during the Pandya rule.

Additional Information

• Pandya Kingdom

• The Pandya Kingdom was one of the three ancient Tamil kingdoms, the other two being the Chola and the Chera kingdoms.

• The Pandyas were known for their contributions to Tamil literature, art, and architecture.

• Their rule is dated back to several centuries BCE, and they were contemporary to other South Indian dynasties like the Cholas and the Cheras.

• The Pandyas were great patrons of the Tamil language and literature, which flourished under their rule.

• Megasthenes

• Megasthenes was a Greek historian and diplomat who served as an ambassador to the court of Chandragupta Maurya in India.

• His work "Indica" provides an account of the Indian subcontinent during the Maurya Empire, including descriptions of the people, culture, and geography.

• Megasthenes' writings are considered valuable historical sources for understanding ancient India.

• Meenakshi Amman Temple

• The Meenakshi Amman Temple is dedicated to Meenakshi, a form of Parvati, and her consort, Sundareshwar, a form of Shiva.

• The temple complex is a significant symbol of South Indian architecture, featuring tall gopurams (gateway towers) adorned with intricate carvings.

• The temple is a major pilgrimage site and attracts millions of visitors and devotees annually.

q: _ authored by Tolkappiyar is the earliest Tamil literature.
solution:
The correct answer is Tolkappiyam.

Key Points

• Tolkappiyam is considered the earliest extant Tamil literary work.

• It was authored by the ancient Tamil scholar Tolkappiyar.

• This work is a comprehensive treatise on Tamil grammar, phonology, morphology, and syntax.

• Tolkappiyam also provides valuable insights into the social and cultural life of ancient Tamil society.

Additional Information

• Ettutogai

• Ettutogai, also known as the Eight Anthologies, is a classical Tamil poetic work.

• It is a collection of eight different anthologies of Tamil poems.

• These poems focus on various themes such as love, valor, and ethics, reflecting the Tamil culture and traditions.

• Kalittogai

• Kalittogai is a classical Tamil poetic work and one of the Eight Anthologies (Ettutogai).

• It comprises 150 poems focusing on the theme of love.

• The poems in Kalittogai are unique in their meter and style, known as Kali meter.

• Narrinai

• Narrinai is also part of the Eight Anthologies (Ettutogai).

• This work consists of 400 poems, primarily focusing on the theme of love.

• Narrinai poems are known for their simplicity and emotional depth.

q: Which of the following kingdoms was divided into subdivisions called Aharas or Rashtras that meant districts?
solution:
The correct answer is Satavahana.

Key Points

• The Satavahana dynasty was an ancient Indian dynasty based in the Deccan region.

• The kingdom was divided into subdivisions called Aharas or Rashtras, which were essentially districts.

• These districts were governed by officers known as Amatyas and Mahamatras.

• The Satavahana administration was highly organized, with efficient management of its various subdivisions.

Additional Information

• Satavahana Dynasty

• The Satavahana dynasty ruled over the Deccan region of India from the 1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE.

• Their rule was marked by the establishment of significant trade routes, both inland and maritime.

• The Satavahanas are known for their contribution to Indian culture, including the promotion of Prakrit and Sanskrit literature.

• They played a crucial role in the cultural and political unification of the Deccan region.

• Administrative Division

• The Satavahana kingdom was divided into various administrative units for effective governance.

• Aharas or Rashtras were the primary administrative divisions, equivalent to modern districts.

• Each Ahara was managed by a set of officers who were responsible for collecting taxes and maintaining law and order.

• This administrative structure helped in the efficient management of the vast territories under Satavahana control.

• Amatyas and Mahamatras

• Amatyas were high-ranking officials who played a crucial role in the administration of the kingdom.

• Mahamatras were officers responsible for various administrative functions, including justice, revenue collection, and public works.

• These officials were appointed based on their abilities and were accountable to the central authority.

• Their roles were critical in maintaining the administrative efficiency and stability of the Satavahana dynasty.

q: According to the Varna system that was prevalent in the Vedic period, which of the following was NOT a Varna?
solution:
The correct answer is Samiti.

Key Points

• The Varna system is a social stratification system found in the Vedic period in ancient India.

• The four main Varnas are Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras.

• Brahmanas were priests and teachers, Kshatriyas were warriors and rulers, Vaishyas were traders, and Shudras were laborers.

• Samiti, however, was not a Varna; it was an assembly of people in the Vedic period used for administrative and deliberative purposes.

Additional Information

• Varna System

• The Varna system is an ancient social hierarchy found in Vedic India, dividing society into four main classes: Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras.

• Brahmanas were considered the highest Varna, responsible for religious rituals, teaching, and maintaining sacred knowledge.

• Kshatriyas were the warrior class and rulers, responsible for protecting and governing the land.

• Vaishyas were the merchant and artisan class, responsible for trade, agriculture, and commerce.

• Shudras were the laborers and service providers, meant to serve the other three Varnas.

• Samiti

• Samiti was not a Varna but an important assembly in the Vedic period.

• It was a gathering of people, often involved in decision-making, administrative matters, and the governance of the community.
