• ​​​On 14 January 1931, on the day of Makar Sankranti, the British military force surrounded and open gunfires on the public present in the peaceful public meeting of freedom fighters at Singhpur Charanpaduka Maidan located on the banks of Urmila river in Chhatarpur district Madhya Pradesh. Charan Paduka Massacre has been called as the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of Madhya Pradesh.

• The Partition of Bengal was announced on 19 July 1905 by the then Viceroy Lord Curzon. It was implemented on 16 October 1905. However, in 1911 it was withdrawn by Lord Hardinge. The stated reason was to ease the administration. But the actual reason was to weaken the growing nationalism in Bengal and break the unity.

• The Chauri Chaura incident took place in British India on February 4, 1922, at Chauri Chaura in the Gorakhpur district of the United Province (modern Uttar Pradesh), when a sizable crowd of demonstrators taking part in the Non-cooperation movement battled with police, who then opened fire.

q: In which of the following years was VD Savarkar sent to Andaman Jail by the British?
solution:
The correct answer is 1911.

Key Points

• Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, also known as Veer Savarkar, was a prominent freedom fighter, social reformer, and writer.

• In 1910, Savarkar was arrested by the British for his involvement in revolutionary activities against the colonial regime.

• He was subsequently tried and sentenced to two life terms of imprisonment totaling fifty years and was deported to the Andaman Islands in 1911.

• The Cellular Jail in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, also known as Kala Pani, was where he was imprisoned. This jail was notorious for its harsh conditions and was used by the British to exile political prisoners.

Additional Information

• Vinayak Damodar Savarkar:

• He was born on May 28, 1883, in Bhagur, a village near Nashik in Maharashtra, India.

• He was a staunch advocate of Hindutva and is credited with founding the ideology.

• Savarkar wrote several books, including "The First War of Indian Independence 1857," which presented the uprising of 1857 as a unified and national effort against British rule.

• After his release from prison, he continued his activities as a social reformer and political activist, although he was kept under strict surveillance by the British authorities.

• Cellular Jail (Kala Pani):

• The Cellular Jail is located in Port Blair, the capital of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

• It was constructed by the British between 1896 and 1906 to exile political prisoners.

• The jail is known for its solitary confinement cells, which were designed to isolate prisoners from each other and prevent them from communicating.

• Many prominent Indian freedom fighters, including Batukeshwar Dutt, Yogendra Shukla, and more, were imprisoned here.

• Today, the Cellular Jail is a national memorial monument.

q: Where was the first official summit of the Non-Aligned movement held?
solution:
The correct answer is Yugoslavia.

Key Points

• The first official summit of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) was held in Belgrade, Yugoslavia, in September 1961.

• The summit was a significant event as it marked the formal establishment of the Non-Aligned Movement.

• The NAM was founded during the Cold War as a group of states that were not formally aligned with or against any major power bloc.

• The movement aimed to create an independent path in world politics that would not be aligned with any major power bloc, particularly the United States or the Soviet Union.

Additional Information

• Non-Aligned Movement (NAM)

• The Non-Aligned Movement is a forum of 120 developing world states that are not formally aligned with or against any major power bloc.

• After the United Nations, it is the largest grouping of states worldwide.

• It originated in the Bandung Conference of 1955, and its first summit was held in Belgrade, Yugoslavia, in 1961.

• Key principles of NAM include mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty, mutual non-aggression, mutual non-interference in domestic affairs, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence.

• Bandung Conference

• The Bandung Conference, also known as the Asian-African Conference, was a meeting of Asian and African states, most of which were newly independent.

• It took place on 18-24 April 1955 in Bandung, Indonesia.

• The conference aimed to promote Afro-Asian economic and cultural cooperation and to oppose colonialism or neocolonialism by any nation.

• The conference was an important step in the establishment of the Non-Aligned Movement.

• Cold War

• The Cold War was a period of geopolitical tension between the Soviet Union and the United States and their respective allies, the Eastern Bloc and the Western Bloc, after World War II.

• The period is generally considered to span from 1947, the year the Truman Doctrine was announced, to 1991, the year the Soviet Union collapsed.

• It was marked by a rivalry between the two superpowers, which did not result in direct large-scale fighting between the two, but involved proxy wars, the arms race, and ideological competition.

q: In which year was the battle of Buxar fought?
solution:
The correct answer is 1764.

Key Points

• The Battle of Buxar was fought on 22 October 1764.

• It was a significant battle between the British East India Company and the combined forces of the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, Nawab of Awadh Shuja-ud-Daula, and Nawab of Bengal Mir Qasim.

• The victory of the British East India Company in the Battle of Buxar solidified their position in India and paved the way for their eventual control over large parts of the Indian subcontinent.

• This battle is considered a pivotal point in Indian history as it marked the beginning of British colonial rule in India.

Additional Information

• British East India Company

• The British East India Company was an English company formed for the exploitation of trade with East and Southeast Asia and India, incorporated by royal charter on December 31, 1600.

• It eventually came to rule large areas of India with its own private armies, exercising military power and assuming administrative functions.

• Mughal Empire

• The Mughal Empire was an empire in the Indian subcontinent, founded in 1526.

• It was established and ruled by a Muslim dynasty with Turko-Mongol Chagatai roots from Central Asia and lasted until the mid-19th century.

• Nawab of Bengal

• The Nawab of Bengal was the hereditary ruler of Bengal and Bihar, with the capital at Murshidabad.

• The last independent Nawab of Bengal, Mir Qasim, was a key figure in the Battle of Buxar.

• Nawab of Awadh

• The Nawab of Awadh was the hereditary ruler of the state of Awadh (Oudh) in northern India.

• Shuja-ud-Daula, the Nawab of Awadh, was one of the key figures in the Battle of Buxar, fighting against the British East India Company.

q: Which among the following was NOT a part of the three sections of the Rigvedic tribe?
solution:
The correct answer is Craftsman.

Key Points

• The three sections of the Rigvedic tribe were Priests (Brahmins), Warriors (Kshatriyas), and Ordinary people (Vaishyas).

• The Rigvedic society was divided into these three main classes or varnas.

• The Craftsman or artisans were not considered a separate class in the Rigvedic social structure.

• These classes or varnas were the foundation of the later Indian caste system.

Additional Information

• Rigvedic Society:

• The Rigveda is one of the oldest known scriptures and forms the basis for the Hindu religion.

• It is composed of hymns dedicated to various deities and reflects the early Vedic civilization.

• The society described in the Rigveda was pastoral and tribal, with a strong emphasis on rituals and sacrifices.

• Varnas System:

• The varna system is a social stratification system mentioned in the Rigveda.

• It classifies society into four varnas: Brahmins (priests), Kshatriyas (warriors), Vaishyas (traders and farmers), and Shudras (servants).

• This system became more rigid in later Vedic society, leading to the development of the caste system.

• Priests (Brahmins):

• Brahmins were responsible for performing religious rituals and maintaining sacred knowledge.

• They held a high status in society due to their spiritual role.

• Warriors (Kshatriyas):

• Kshatriyas were the protectors and rulers of the tribe.

• They were responsible for governance, warfare, and maintaining law and order.

• Ordinary People (Vaishyas):

• Vaishyas were engaged in agriculture, trade, and commerce.

• They formed the economic backbone of the society.

q: The Aryans lived in the land known as ‘Sapta Sindhu’ (Land of the Seven Rivers). Which of the following was NOT a part of it?
solution:
The correct answer is Shipra.

Key Points

• The Aryans lived in the region known as 'Sapta Sindhu', which means the Land of the Seven Rivers.

• The seven rivers that were part of 'Sapta Sindhu' are the Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej, and Saraswati.

• Shipra is not one of these seven rivers and is therefore not part of the 'Sapta Sindhu'.

• Shipra is a river in the central Indian state of Madhya Pradesh and is famous for the city of Ujjain which is one of the locations for the Kumbh Mela.

Additional Information

• Sapta Sindhu

• Sapta Sindhu refers to the region of the seven rivers which were mentioned in ancient Indian texts, especially the Rigveda.

• The seven rivers include the Indus (Sindhu), Jhelum (Vitasta), Chenab (Asikni), Ravi (Parushni), Beas (Vipas), Sutlej (Shutudri), and Saraswati (which has now dried up).

• This region is considered the cradle of the early Vedic civilization.

• The term 'Sapta Sindhu' is often associated with the Punjab region of modern-day India and Pakistan.

• Indus River

• One of the longest rivers in the world, flowing through China (Tibet), India, and Pakistan.

• It was the backbone of the Indus Valley Civilization, one of the world's oldest urban cultures.

• The river is also known as Sindhu in Sanskrit.

• Jhelum River

• Originates from the Indian-administered territory of Jammu and Kashmir.

• Flows through the Kashmir Valley and Pakistan, eventually joining the Chenab River.

• It is also known as Vitasta in ancient texts.

• Shipra River

• Located in the central Indian state of Madhya Pradesh.

• It is famous for the city of Ujjain, which is one of the locations for the Kumbh Mela, a major Hindu pilgrimage.

• The Shipra is not part of the 'Sapta Sindhu' and was not associated with the Aryan civilization in the same context.

q:
With reference of Ajivikas, consider the following statements.

a) Makkhali Gosala was the prominent teacher of this sect.

b) Ajivikas believed in fatalism.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution:
The correct answer is Both a and b.

Key Points

• Makkhali Gosala was indeed the prominent teacher of the Ajivika sect, which is a fundamental point in understanding the history of this ascetic sect.

• The Ajivikas were known for their belief in fatalism, the idea that all events are predetermined and therefore inevitable.

• The sect was a contemporary of Buddhism and Jainism and had a significant influence during the time of the Mauryan Empire.

• Ajivikas followed a strict ascetic lifestyle and believed in the concept of niyati (destiny).

Additional Information

• Ajivikas:

• The Ajivikas were an ascetic sect that emerged in ancient India around the same time as Buddhism and Jainism. They believed in the doctrine of predetermination, where every event is preordained and humans are powerless to change their destiny.

• Makkhali Gosala: He was one of the key figures in the Ajivika sect. His teachings emphasized the power of fate over individual effort.

• The teachings of the Ajivikas were based on the principle of niyati, which means destiny. This doctrine suggested that everything in the world was predetermined and fixed, and human efforts to change their fate were futile.

• The Ajivikas practiced extreme asceticism and renunciation, similar to other contemporary religious movements like Jainism.

• Fatalism:

• Fatalism is the philosophical doctrine suggesting that all events are predetermined and inevitable, a belief that is central to the Ajivika philosophy.

• It implies that human actions have no effect on the future, which is already decided by destiny or fate.

• This belief can lead to a deterministic outlook on life, where individuals accept whatever happens without trying to change their circumstances.

• In the context of Ajivikas, this meant that their ascetic practices were part of adhering to their predetermined path.

q: Which of the following Sultans of Delhi primarily adopted a policy of consolidation rather than expansion?
solution:
The correct answer is Balban.

Key Points

• Ghiyas ud din Balban was one of the most prominent Sultans of the Slave Dynasty in India.

• He ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1266 to 1287.

• Balban primarily focused on consolidating his empire rather than expanding it.

• He implemented strong administrative policies and maintained a robust military to ensure internal stability and defense against external threats.

Additional Information

• Ibrahim Lodi

• Ibrahim Lodi was the last Sultan of the Lodi dynasty, ruling from 1517 to 1526.

• He attempted to maintain and expand the empire but faced internal revolts and was ultimately defeated by Babur in the First Battle of Panipat.

• Alauddin Khalji

• Alauddin Khalji ruled from 1296 to 1316.

• He is known for his aggressive expansionist policies and successful military campaigns in the Deccan and northern India.

• He also implemented significant economic and administrative reforms.

• Bahlol Lodi

• Bahlol Lodi was the founder of the Lodi dynasty and ruled from 1451 to 1489.

• He focused on consolidating his power in the region and laid the foundation for the Lodi rule in Delhi.

q: Which of the following battles was fought between Babur and Rana Sanga in 1527?
solution:
The correct answer is Battle of Khanwa.

Key Points

• The Battle of Khanwa was fought on 16 March 1527 between the forces of Babur and Rana Sanga of Mewar.

• This battle was a decisive victory for Babur, which consolidated his rule over North India.

• Babur employed tactics such as the use of cannons and the Tulughma strategy, which played a crucial role in his victory.

• The battle marked the end of the Rajput confederacy's resistance against Babur and paved the way for the establishment of the Mughal Empire in India.

Additional Information

• Battle of Bayana

• It was fought in 1527 between Babur and the Rajput forces of Rana Sanga before the Battle of Khanwa.

• Babur's victory at Bayana was crucial in weakening the Rajput forces before the major confrontation at Khanwa.

• Second Battle of Panipat

• This battle was fought in 1556 between the forces of the Mughal emperor Akbar and Hemu, the Hindu king of Delhi.

• Akbar's victory at Panipat consolidated Mughal power in India.

• Battle of Chanderi

• Fought in 1528, it was another confrontation between Babur and the Rajput forces led by Medini Rai of Chanderi.

• This battle resulted in a decisive victory for Babur and further strengthened his control over North India.

q: Who among the following founded the Pala dynasty in 8th Century CE?
solution:
The correct answer is Gopala.

Key Points

• Gopala was the founder of the Pala dynasty in the 8th century CE.

• He was elected by a group of regional chieftains to bring order in a period of anarchy in Bengal.

• Gopala established the Pala dynasty, which ruled over the Bengal and Bihar regions for about four centuries.

• His reign marked the beginning of a period of stability and expansion in the region.

Additional Information

• Pala Dynasty

• The Pala Dynasty was a major dynasty in the history of the Indian subcontinent, primarily ruling over the Bengal and Bihar regions.

• The term 'Pala' means 'protector' and was used as a suffix to the names of all Pala monarchs.

• The Pala rulers were patrons of Mahayana Buddhism and played a significant role in its spread to Tibet, Bhutan, and other parts of Southeast Asia.

• The dynasty is known for its contributions to art, architecture, and education, including the establishment of the Vikramashila and Nalanda universities.

• Dharmapala

• Dharmapala was the son of Gopala and the second ruler of the Pala dynasty.

• He expanded the empire significantly and was known for his support of Buddhism and educational institutions.

• His reign is considered a golden period for the Pala dynasty.

• Devapala

• Devapala was another significant ruler of the Pala dynasty and is believed to be the successor of Dharmapala.

• He continued to expand the empire and maintained its dominance over the northern Indian subcontinent.

• Devapala is also known for his patronage of Buddhism and his support for the Nalanda and Vikramashila universities.

• Ramapala

• Ramapala was one of the later rulers of the Pala dynasty and is often credited with reviving the dynasty's fortunes in the 12th century.

• He is known for his administrative reforms and efforts to consolidate the empire.

• His reign is detailed in the historical text "Ramacharitam," written by Sandhyakar Nandi.

q: Which Act was passed by the British Parliament in the year 1773 AD to regulate the activities of the East India Company?
solution:
The correct answer is Regulating Act.

Key Points

• The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first step taken by the British Parliament to control and regulate the affairs of the East India Company in India.

• It marked the beginning of British parliamentary control over the East India Company and its administration in India.

• The Act provided for the establishment of a Supreme Court at Calcutta (now Kolkata) to administer justice.

• The Governor of Bengal was elevated to the position of Governor-General of Bengal, with supervisory authority over the presidencies of Madras and Bombay.

Additional Information

• Pitt's India Act

• Passed in 1784, this Act was intended to address the deficiencies of the Regulating Act of 1773.

• It established a dual system of control by setting up a Board of Control to oversee the political affairs while the Court of Directors retained control over commercial affairs.

• This Act allowed the British government to have greater control over the administration of India.

• Indian Slavery Act

• Passed in 1843, this Act aimed to abolish slavery in British India.

• It made the sale, purchase, or transfer of slaves illegal and provided for the protection of the rights of those who had been enslaved.

• Age of Consent Act

• Enacted in 1891, this Act raised the age of consent for girls from 10 to 12 years in all jurisdictions, whether Hindu or Muslim.

• It was aimed at addressing the issue of child marriage and the associated health risks for young girls.

q: The Permanent Settlement came into operation in which of the following years?
solution:
The correct answer is 1793.

Key Points

• The Permanent Settlement was introduced by the East India Company during the tenure of Lord Cornwallis in 1793.

• It was an agreement between the East India Company and Bengali landlords to fix revenues to be raised from land.

• This system was primarily implemented in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.

• Under this system, the Zamindars were recognized as the owners of the land and were responsible for collecting and paying the fixed revenue to the Company.

Additional Information

• Permanent Settlement

• The Permanent Settlement was also known as the Zamindari System.

• The Zamindars were required to pay a fixed amount of revenue to the East India Company, irrespective of the agricultural yield.

• This system aimed to ensure a stable revenue for the Company and incentivize Zamindars to improve agricultural practices.

• However, it led to the exploitation of peasants and did not significantly improve agricultural productivity.

• Lord Cornwallis

• He was the Governor-General of India from 1786 to 1793.

• He introduced several reforms in the administration, judiciary, and revenue systems of India.

• The Cornwallis Code, introduced in 1793, aimed to overhaul the administrative structure in British India.

• He is credited with laying the foundation of a structured administration in India.

• Impact of Permanent Settlement

• The system led to the emergence of a new class of landlords who were loyal to the British.

• It created a stark divide between the Zamindars and the peasants, leading to widespread poverty and indebtedness among the latter.

• The rigidity of the revenue demand often led to the transfer of land ownership and distress sales.

• The system was criticized for its failure to promote agricultural development and for exacerbating social inequalities.

q: In 1936, The Independent Labour Party was founded by .
solution:
The correct answer is BR Ambedkar.

Key Points

• Dr. BR Ambedkar was a prominent Indian jurist, economist, and social reformer who campaigned against social discrimination towards the untouchables (Dalits).

• He was the principal architect of the Constitution of India and served as the first Law Minister of India.

• In 1936, Dr. BR Ambedkar founded the Independent Labour Party, which aimed to secure social justice and eradicate social inequalities.

• The party contested the Bombay Legislative Assembly elections held in 1937 and won 15 seats.

Additional Information

• Independent Labour Party (ILP)

• The Independent Labour Party was established by BR Ambedkar on 15 August 1936 in Bombay.

• The ILP was formed to address the issues faced by the working class and the marginalized sections of society, particularly the Dalits.

• The party's manifesto emphasized the need for state socialism in the sphere of industry and agriculture.

• It also advocated for labor rights, including fair wages, decent working conditions, and social security measures for workers.

• BR Ambedkar

• Born on 14 April 1891, Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was a prolific scholar and an influential leader of the Dalit community in India.

• He played a crucial role in drafting the Indian Constitution and was a strong advocate for the rights of the oppressed and marginalized.

• Ambedkar's efforts led to significant social reforms, including the abolition of untouchability and the promotion of education and employment opportunities for Dalits.

• He embraced Buddhism in 1956 along with many of his followers, which marked a significant movement in the Dalit community towards religious and social empowerment.

• Social Reform Movements in India

• Social reform movements in India aimed at eradicating social evils and injustices prevalent in society, such as caste discrimination, gender inequality, and child marriage.

• Prominent social reformers included Raja Ram Mohan Roy, who worked towards the abolition of Sati, and Jyotirao Phule, who fought for the rights of the lower castes and women's education.

• These movements laid the foundation for a more equitable and just society in India by challenging traditional norms and advocating for progressive changes.

• The contributions of leaders like BR Ambedkar were instrumental in shaping modern India's social and political landscape.

q: Being the President of the Indian National Congress, who among the following had called for complete independence from the British Raj in 1929?
solution:
The correct answer is Jawaharlal Nehru.

Key Points

• Jawaharlal Nehru was a prominent leader of the Indian National Congress and a key figure in the Indian independence movement.

• He was the one who called for complete independence from British rule during the Lahore session of the Indian National Congress in 1929.

• The demand for complete independence (Purna Swaraj) was officially adopted by the Indian National Congress at this session.

• The resolution for complete independence was passed on December 31, 1929, and January 26, 1930, was declared as the Independence Day, which was later celebrated as Republic Day after India became independent.

Additional Information

• Indian National Congress (INC)

• The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 and played a significant role in the Indian independence movement against British rule.

• It was the principal party behind the demand for self-rule and later complete independence from British colonialism.

• Leaders like Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, Subhas Chandra Bose, and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel were prominent figures associated with INC.

• Lahore Session of 1929

• The Lahore session of the INC in December 1929 was a pivotal moment in the Indian independence movement.

• During this session, the demand for Purna Swaraj (complete independence) was officially adopted.

• Jawaharlal Nehru was elected as the President of the INC during this session.

• The INC decided to celebrate January 26, 1930, as Independence Day, marking the beginning of a direct action campaign for complete independence.

• Purna Swaraj (Complete Independence)

• Purna Swaraj means complete self-rule or full independence from British rule.

• The resolution for Purna Swaraj was a declaration that the Indian people would fight for complete independence and not settle for anything less.

• This declaration intensified the struggle for independence and led to various civil disobedience movements and protests against British rule.

• Republic Day

• January 26 was chosen as the Republic Day to honor the date on which the Declaration of Independence was proclaimed in 1930.

• On January 26, 1950, the Constitution of India came into effect, making India a sovereign, democratic republic.

• Republic Day is celebrated every year with grand parades and festivities across the country.

q: The book 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' was written by .
solution:
The correct answer is Dadabhai Naoroji.

Key Points

• Dadabhai Naoroji, also known as the "Grand Old Man of India," was a prominent Indian political leader and social reformer.

• He was one of the founding members of the Indian National Congress and a strong advocate for India's independence from British rule.

• In his book "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India," Naoroji presented a detailed critique of the British economic policies in India, arguing that they were responsible for the widespread poverty in the country.

• Naoroji's work laid the foundation for the Indian nationalist movement and inspired future leaders like Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru.

Additional Information

• Poverty and Un-British Rule in India

• This book, published in 1901, is a seminal work by Dadabhai Naoroji in which he systematically examined the economic impacts of British rule on India.

• Naoroji introduced the concept of "Drain Theory," which argued that a significant portion of India's wealth was being drained to Britain without adequate returns, leading to persistent poverty in India.

• The book provided statistical evidence to support Naoroji's claims, making a compelling case for economic reforms and self-governance.

• It was one of the first works to use economic analysis to critique colonial policies, influencing both Indian and British policymakers.

• Dadabhai Naoroji

• He was born on 4th September 1825 in Mumbai and was educated at Elphinstone College.

• Naoroji was also the first Indian to be elected to the British Parliament, representing the Liberal Party for Finsbury Central from 1892 to 1895.

• He played a key role in bringing the economic grievances of Indians to the attention of the British public and Parliament.

• Besides his political career, Naoroji was an educator, co-founding the University of Mumbai, and a businessman involved in the cotton trade.

• Indian National Congress (INC)

• Founded in 1885, the INC was the first modern nationalist movement to emerge in the British Empire in Asia and Africa.

• The Congress became the principal leader of the Indian independence movement, with its influence spreading from the Indian subcontinent to the rest of the world.

• It played a significant role in the independence struggle, leading to India gaining independence in 1947.

• Prominent leaders associated with the Congress include Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, and Subhas Chandra Bose.

q: Who among the following was the President of the Belgaum Session of the Indian National Congress held in 1924?
solution:
The correct answer is Mahatma Gandhi.

Key Points

• Mahatma Gandhi presided over the Belgaum session of the Indian National Congress in 1924.

• This was the only session of the Indian National Congress that Mahatma Gandhi ever presided over.

• The session was held from 26th to 27th December 1924 in Belgaum, Karnataka.

• Gandhi's presidency at this session was significant as it was a period of transition in the Indian freedom struggle, with the rise of new leaders and ideologies.

Additional Information

• Indian National Congress (INC)

• The Indian National Congress (INC) was founded in 1885 by Allan Octavian Hume, Dadabhai Naoroji, and Dinshaw Wacha.

• It played a key role in the Indian independence movement against British rule.

• The INC was the principal leader of the Indian independence movement, fighting for self-governance and full sovereignty from the British Empire.

• Mahatma Gandhi

• Mahatma Gandhi, born as Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, was an Indian lawyer, anti-colonial nationalist, and political ethicist who employed nonviolent resistance to lead the successful campaign for India's independence from British rule.

• He is also known for his philosophy of nonviolence (ahimsa) and his role in various social reforms in India.

• Gandhi's leadership and strategies in the freedom struggle inspired numerous movements for civil rights and freedom across the world.

• Belgaum

• Belgaum, officially known as Belagavi, is a city in the Indian state of Karnataka.

• It is known for its historical importance and was chosen as the location for the 1924 session of the Indian National Congress.

q: Mahendravarman I who wrote Mattavilasa-prahasana is related to which of the following ruling dynasties?
solution:
The correct answer is Pallava.

Key Points

• Mahendravarman I was a ruler of the Pallava dynasty who ruled over the southern part of India during the early 7th century.

• He is known for his patronage of arts and architecture, particularly for initiating the rock-cut architecture in Mahabalipuram.

• Mahendravarman I was a versatile scholar and a playwright, and he composed the famous Sanskrit play Mattavilasa-prahasana (The Delight of the Drunkards).

• The Pallavas were instrumental in the promotion of Tamil literature and culture, and they contributed significantly to the growth of Dravidian architecture.

Additional Information

• Maitraka Dynasty

• The Maitrakas ruled parts of present-day Gujarat from the late 5th century to the 8th century.

• They were known for their patronage of learning and religion, particularly Buddhism and Jainism.

• Pushyabhuti Dynasty

• The Pushyabhuti dynasty, also known as the Vardhana dynasty, ruled parts of northern India in the 6th and 7th centuries.

• The most notable ruler of this dynasty was Harsha Vardhana, who extended his empire across much of North India.

• Chalukya Dynasty

• The Chalukyas were a major dynasty that ruled large parts of southern and central India between the 6th and the 12th centuries.

• They are known for their contributions to art, architecture, and literature, particularly in the Deccan region.

q: The real name of Babur, the founder of Mughal dynasty in India was:
solution:
The correct answer is Zahiruddin Muhammad.

Key Points

• Zahiruddin Muhammad Babur was the founder of the Mughal Empire in India.

• He was born on 14 February 1483 in Andijan, in present-day Uzbekistan.

• Babur was a descendant of Timur on his father's side and Genghis Khan on his mother's side, giving him a prestigious lineage.

• He established the Mughal Empire in 1526 after his victory in the First Battle of Panipat.

Additional Information

• Babur

• Babur was a conqueror from Central Asia who, following a series of setbacks, finally succeeded in laying the basis for the Mughal dynasty in the Indian subcontinent and became the first Mughal emperor.

• He was known for his military ability, leadership, and cultural contributions.

• His memoirs, known as the Baburnama, provide a detailed account of his life and the political conditions of his time.

• Mughal Dynasty

• The Mughal Empire was an early-modern empire in South Asia. For some two centuries, the empire stretched from the outer fringes of the Indus basin, northern Afghanistan, and Kashmir in the northwest to the highlands of present-day Assam and Bangladesh in the east, and to the uplands of the Deccan plateau in south India.

• The Mughal Empire brought about a significant change in the culture, economy, and architecture of the Indian subcontinent.

• It is particularly noted for its contributions to art and architecture, such as the Taj Mahal.

• First Battle of Panipat

• The First Battle of Panipat was fought on 21 April 1526, between the invading forces of Babur and the Lodi Empire.

• This battle marked the beginning of the Mughal Empire in India.

• Babur's use of artillery and innovative tactics were pivotal in his victory.

q: A large number of words are derived from the word 'Go' meaning cow. A wealthy person was known as _ in Vedic times.
solution:

q: The Pratiharas who first had their capital at Bhinmal gained prominence during the rule of:
solution:
The correct answer is Nagabhatta I.

Key Points

• Nagabhatta I was the founder of the Pratihara dynasty and reigned around the early 8th century.

• He is credited with defending the western frontier of India against Arab invasions, particularly from the Umayyad Caliphate.

• Nagabhatta I established Bhinmal (modern-day Rajasthan) as his capital, marking the beginning of the Pratihara Empire's prominence.

• Under his leadership, the Pratihara dynasty began to rise as a significant power in northern India.

Additional Information

• Pratihara Dynasty:

• The Pratihara dynasty was an important power in northern India from the 6th to the 11th centuries.

• They are known for their role in protecting India from external invasions, particularly from Arab forces.

• The Pratiharas were known for their patronage of art and architecture, contributing significantly to the cultural heritage of India.

• Bhinmal:

• Bhinmal, also known as Srimal, was an ancient city located in the present-day Jalore district of Rajasthan.

• It served as the early capital of the Pratihara dynasty before they moved their capital to Kannauj.

• Bhinmal was a center of learning and culture, producing notable scholars like Brahmagupta.

• Umayyad Caliphate:

• The Umayyad Caliphate was the second of the four major caliphates established after the death of Muhammad.

• Under the Umayyads, the Muslim empire expanded rapidly, and their incursions reached into the Indian subcontinent.

• The Pratiharas, under Nagabhatta I, were able to resist these invasions and establish themselves as a formidable power.
